t: LeetCode 2006 — Count Number of Pairs With Absolute Difference K
o:
## Understanding the problem

We count index pairs (i, j) with i < j whose absolute difference |nums[i] − nums[j]| equals k. The constraints are tiny — at most 200 elements with values up to 100 — so even examining every pair (about 2·10^4 comparisons) finishes instantly, but the problem also has a neat one-pass hash-map solution worth knowing.

Example walkthrough: nums = [1,2,2,1], k = 1 → qualifying pairs are indices (0,1),(0,2),(1,3),(2,3), giving 4. For nums = [3,2,1,5,4], k = 2 the pairs are (3,1),(3,5),(2,4) — three of them, matching the expected output. For nums = [1,3], k = 3 nothing matches, so the answer is 0.
k: |nums[i] − nums[j]| == k means the pair works exactly when one element is k larger than the other.
Because k >= 1, x − k ≠ x + k, so summing cnt[x − k] + cnt[x + k] never double-counts a partner.
A running frequency map converts the O(n^2) pairwise scan into a single pass.

a.i: Enumerate all pairs with the outer index smaller than the inner one and test the absolute difference directly. This is the definition translated to code — impossible to get wrong, and perfectly adequate for n <= 200.
s: For each i from 0 to n−1, for each j from i+1 to n−1, increment ans when abs(nums[i] − nums[j]) equals k.
a.t: O(n^2) — every ordered-by-index pair is inspected once

a.i: Scan left to right keeping counts of values already seen. When processing x, every earlier value equal to x − k or x + k forms a valid pair with the current occurrence, so add cnt[x − k] + cnt[x + k], then record x itself. Each pair is counted exactly once — at the moment its right element arrives.
s: Create an empty frequency map cnt.
For each x in nums: add cnt[x − k] + cnt[x + k] to ans.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant-time hash lookups
a.sp: O(min(n, U)) where U is the number of distinct values (at most 100 here)

w:
## Wrap-up

Mention the brute force first (the constraints make it legitimate), then offer the hash-map pass as the scalable answer. Pitfalls: counting ordered pairs instead of i < j pairs; forgetting both x − k and x + k lookups; special-casing k = 0 unnecessarily (constraints forbid it, but note that then cnt[x] alone would be the term and the same code breaks due to self-matching — worth flagging in discussion). An equivalent closed form builds the full frequency table first and sums cnt[v] · cnt[v + k] over all v. Follow-ups: huge arrays (sort + two pointers), negative values (hash map handles them unchanged), or streaming input.
